name: Emeka Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own a small recording studio called Zhang Sound, in a converted garage behind the house my wife Grace and I bought. I record gospel choirs, local bands, and a lot of podcasts these days. On Sundays I play bass at our church, and twice a month I gig with a soul covers band. I've also got an apprentice, Kofi, who's nineteen and learning the trade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of the studio work is AI already?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot of the boring part. I use AI every day to clean up noise, edit podcasts, and get a first master that I then fix by ear. I built Zhang Sound (his studio) with a bank loan and my own hands, and I'll use any tool that helps me keep it. Clients pay for the result, not for how many hours I suffered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and that's that. Anyone who works smart will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. I keep my clients and my tools keep getting slightly better. The podcast work stays steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing Zhang Sound. Pay off the rest of the studio loan this year. Keep training Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things are going well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is left on the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight thousand. I could clear it now from savings. Clearing the studio loan this year would mean everything in that garage belongs to Grace (his wife) and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Kofi learn from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mic placement, how to talk to a nervous singer, how to run a session on time. The software he picks up faster than me.

I'd say anyone who **works smart** will do fine in this world.
think: My **clients stay** and my tools keep improving slightly.
The **podcast work** stays steady, so the studio keeps paying its way.
do: Pay off the last **eight thousand** of the studio loan this year.
Keep growing **Zhang Sound** and training Kofi.
S0.quote: Clearing the studio loan this year would mean everything in that garage belongs to Grace (his wife) and me.
fieldNote: Emeka **owns his business** and uses AI daily, so a plateau suits him.
He values **ownership**: clearing the loan matters to him.
His apprentice **Kofi** reflects his belief in learning a trade.

steps.text: Pay off the last eight thousand of the studio loan
Keep training Kofi in mic placement and running sessions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work. Businesses that use these tools will win, and the ones that don't will lose. That's the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the easy podcast editing will go. Podcasters will do it themselves with an app. But choirs and bands still need a room, mics and someone who knows what he's doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift Zhang Sound toward live recording sessions and choirs. I'd automate everything else, editing and first masters, so I can take more clients. And I'd train Kofi in live sound, because that's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. But I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your income is podcast editing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third. A third of Zhang Sound's (his studio's) money comes from editing podcasts, and I'd expect most of that to walk out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame anyone for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's the market. If I can't offer something better than an app, I don't deserve the client.

**Choirs and bands** still need a room and someone skilled.
do: Shift Zhang Sound toward **live recording** sessions and choirs.
**Automate** editing and first masters to take more clients.

fieldNote: Emeka **blames no one**: losing clients to apps is the market.
He'd **automate** his own thinking work to take on more hands-on sessions.
His **ownership** and adaptability make him feel in control.

steps.text: Automate podcast editing and first masters with AI tools
Market Zhang Sound to choirs and bands for live sessions
Train Kofi to run live sound at gigs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but businesses and families have to adapt. I'd say people should not sit and wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think most of the studio business goes. If AI makes a perfect record from a phone recording by 2028, why would a band pay me? Choirs might still come for the room, but it's a small market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell some of the expensive gear while it still has value. I'd turn the garage into a rehearsal and live venue space for small events. I'd look for live sound work, which is hands-on until robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I built this with my own hands and it could be gone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Kofi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. I'd have to tell Kofi, my nineteen-year-old apprentice, that the trade I'm teaching him might not exist in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a dental hygienist. Hands-on, so she'd be okay for a while. We'd live on her pay if we had to.

I'd say people shouldn't sit and wait for **handouts** from anyone.

**Choirs** might still come for the room, but it's a small market.
do: Sell some **expensive gear** while it still holds value.
Turn the garage into a **rehearsal and live venue** space.

steps.text: Sell the most expensive studio microphones and preamps

Look for live sound engineering work at venues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for business owners to plan. I'd talk about it with other studio owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio still mostly goes, around 2031. But five years lets me plan the shift instead of scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the studio for three years and use AI to take more clients. Then I'd convert the garage into a live space. And I'd train Kofi in live sound and help him find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still take on apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but for live sound, not studio work. A trade worth teaching in five years is one where you have to stand in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversion cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fifteen thousand. Savings would cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. The market will sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm thirty-seven. I'd have grown the studio, then moved into live events gradually. Maybe children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow Zhang Sound now, maybe hire a second apprentice. Use AI for everything that saves time. And in five or six years, start the move into live events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps the unease there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not knowing what a studio is worth in ten years. Zhang Sound (his studio) might be worth nothing in ten years, so I'd take the money it makes now and put it into something I can stand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Something you can stand in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Property. A building for live events, or a share in one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the studio could be gone before I'd built anything else. What would help is fewer rules and lower taxes for small businesses trying to change, and apprenticeships in trades that need people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about apprentices. Young people need trades, and I worry about what Kofi's generation will learn.

headlineQuote: I built Zhang Sound (his studio) with a bank loan and my own hands, and I'll use any tool that helps me keep it.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** bassist who owns Zhang Sound, a small studio in a converted garage.
He's **traditional** and pro-market, uses AI daily, and blames no one for change.
He'd **automate** his own thinking work and move toward live, hands-on events.
Fast AGI **alarms** him because his business could vanish in two years.
He worries about his apprentice **Kofi** and young people needing trades.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the studio could be gone before he built anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and fewer rules for small businesses, and **apprenticeships** in hands-on trades.
